content:
# Semantic-Anchored Checkpointing with Suffix-Only Re-Prefill: Edge Cases

## The governing invariant (everything follows from this)

Causal attention means the K/V entry at position *j* is a function of tokens *x₀…xⱼ*. An edit landing at position *e* therefore taints every cached position ≥ *e*. There is **no sound partial splice, no suffix transplant, no "patch the middle"** — the only sound reuse is an exact token-id prefix match, resumed from a verified anchor. Semantic anchors exist solely to push that resume point as late as possible while remaining provably valid. Every failure mode below is a violation of one clause of that sentence.

---

## A. Identity failures — the prefix you think you preserved isn't

1. **Non-canonical serialization.** Timestamps, UUIDs, request IDs, dict iteration order, float formatting (`0.1` vs `0.10000000000000001`), locale decimal separators baked into the context stream. Two logically identical states serialize to different bytes → LCP terminates early → full re-prefill of a "unchanged" prefix. Guard: canonical serializer, frozen-at-write volatile fields, snapshot test that re-serializing a loaded checkpoint is byte-identical.
2. **Injected clock in the system prompt.** `"Current time: …"` rendered per call means every call has a different prefix. The cache hit rate is zero by construction and nobody notices because it degrades gracefully. Freeze a per-session genesis timestamp or expose time as a tool.
3. **Unicode normalization drift.** Editor writes NFD, serializer emits NFC → first non-ASCII character becomes a false divergence point. Normalize once at ingest; the stored byte stream is the only truth.
4. **Chat-template re-rendering.** Re-running the full conversation through the template each call means a template bump (even whitespace) invalidates every checkpoint. Worse: templates that re-sort tool schemas or interleave system content mid-stream cause divergence *inside* an apparently stable region. Pin template hash per session; freeze tool-schema blocks at first emission, never re-sort.
5. **Tool-result retry mutation.** Retry writes fresh bytes (new timestamps, new IDs) into the same slot → LCP breaks at that message. Policy: first result is frozen; retries append as new messages. Otherwise retry storms silently convert your suffix-only system into a full-reprefill system.
6. **Multimodal payload instability.** Image re-decode with different EXIF rotation, vision-preprocessing version bump, PDF re-rasterization → different embeddings behind identical "text." Anchor hashes must cover binary payload digests and preprocessing version, not just string content.
7. **Regime change without fingerprint.** Model weight update, engine container retag (kernel numerics shift), KV dtype change (fp16→fp8), LoRA adapter swap mid-session — all change K/V values for identical token ids. Mixing blocks across regimes is silent corruption. Checkpoints carry `(weights_fingerprint, engine_build, kv_dtype, adapter_id, template_hash)`; any mismatch → full invalidate, no exceptions.

## B. Alignment failures — right idea, wrong boundary

8. **String-level LCP instead of token-level.** Character-level common prefix can land mid-multibyte character or mid-BPE merge; re-tokenizing from there yields a *different token sequence* than the original stream. Compute LCP over token ids from the recorded token log, never over strings.
9. **Partial-block reuse.** Paged attention blocks (say 16 tokens): the divergence falls mid-block, but the block hash matches because the *stored* block was hashed whole. Reusing it imports post-divergence tokens into the prefix. Rule: a block is reusable only if it lies **entirely** within the validated LCP; the straddling block's tail is recomputed.
10. **Position/RoPE offset error on resume.** Suffix prefill must continue at the anchor's absolute position. Restarting position ids at 0, or off-by-one at the seam, produces plausible-looking garbage. Assert `resume_position == anchor.position` as a hard check, not a convention.
11. **Pending-tail ambiguity.** Streaming generation leaves a dangling partial token in a flush buffer. Checkpoints taken pre-flush and LCP computations that disagree about whether the tail is included diverge by one token — which invalidates everything downstream. Rule: anchors exist only at flushed, finalized boundaries; the pending tail is never part of any anchor.
12. **Attention-sink / sliding-window truncation.** Resuming from an anchor that drops the sink tokens (or window-prime tokens) breaks generation outright for architectures that require them resident. Know your architecture's mandatory-resident set; anchors never cut below it.

## C. Lifetime and concurrency failures — own-iron means you own the allocator

13. **Eviction race.** Checkpoint holds block references by hash but doesn't pin them; the pool evicts between checkpoint commit and suffix prefill. Outcomes range from crash to silent full-recompute fallback. Refcount every referenced block at checkpoint creation; a fallback to full recompute must be logged and counted, never silent.
14. **Fork/branch refcount bugs.** Basecamp operators fork heads to experiment. Blocks die only when *no head in any lineage* references them. Over-free → a sibling branch reads freed blocks (corruption that surfaces far from the cause). Under-free → GPU OOM hours later. Per-block atomic refcounts, generation-tagged GC, and a periodic audit reconciling live-head sets against pinned sets.
15. **Two writers, one context.** Multiple panes/scripts mutating the session file. Checkpoints stamped under writer A's epoch are meaningless under writer B's bytes. Single-writer discipline or MVCC epochs; stale-epoch checkpoints are unusable, full stop.
16. **Crash window between context commit and checkpoint commit.** Orphan checkpoints are harmless; an advanced live pointer without a durable checkpoint is not. WAL with the ordering: persist checkpoint (bytes + anchor index + block refs + journal cursor) atomically → then advance live pointer. Recovery rolls the live pointer back to the newest durable anchor.
17. **Torn writes on the checkpoint store.** Own-iron disk, no vendor durability story. Checksum every checkpoint record; a corrupt anchor index falls back to the *previous* anchor, never to a partially-written one.

## D. Semantic-layer failures — the context is fine, the world isn't

18. **Side-effect/context desync.** The worst one. Rollback restores context to T, but tools fired up to T+k already executed (email sent, file written, API called). Naive resume re-executes them. Anchors must align with the side-effect journal: an anchor is restorable only if every effect ≤ that anchor is journaled committed-and-idempotent. Tools carry idempotency keys; the journal cursor lives *inside* the checkpoint record.
19. **Anchors in non-quiescent regions.** An anchor after a partially-emitted tool-invocation JSON, or mid-plan-step, is a trap: the repair/retry path rewrites that region and the anchor rots. Quiescence definition: completed assistant turn, committed tool result, finalized step. Nothing else.
20. **Executing calls from discarded context.** Edit lands mid-stream; the discarded suffix contained a parsed tool call. If anything executes it, you've acted on invalidated provenance. Discard the parse with the tokens.
21. **Orphaned async results.** Rollback past an issued tool call; the result arrives afterward for a call that no longer exists. Quarantine it, attach to the journal, surface to the operator. Never auto-inject into the historical slot it "belongs" to.
22. **No-op edits forcing work.** An edit that serializes byte-identically must trigger zero prefill and zero model call. Detect and short-circuit; don't burn a decode cycle "confirming."
23. **Shrinkage mishandling.** Deletions and replacements mean the "new suffix" is a divergent continuation, not an append. Systems assuming monotonic growth mis-handle this. Compaction/summarization is a wholesale rewrite — LCP ≈ 0 — and must be declared as a rebuild with a discontinuity marker, never laundered through the incremental-edit path. Never compact mid-tool-loop; do it at idle.

## E. What must never happen (hard invariants)

- **Never** resume prefill from a cache keyed by anything other than the exact token-id prefix of the current context — not semantic equivalence, not fuzzy match, not "close enough."
- **Never** execute a side effect whose provenance traces to a discarded suffix.
- **Never** mutate a checkpoint in place; heads are immutable, edits create new lineages.
- **Never** place an anchor outside a quiescent, flushed, journaled boundary.
- **Never** mix KV blocks across weight fingerprints, engine builds, dtypes, adapters, or template versions.
- **Never** report a cache hit when you fell back to full recompute — telemetry honesty is load-bearing, because a silent fallback masks the exact bug class this design exists to catch.
- **Never** reference unpinned blocks in a durable checkpoint.
- **Never** reuse a KV block at a shifted position offset (breaks absolute-position/RoPE assumptions).
- **Never** let compaction masquerade as an append.

## F. Boundaries — where the technique honestly degrades

- **Head edits.** Edit at message 3 of 40 → deepest surviving anchor is near genesis → full rebuild. Savings scale with edit depth; head-heavy edit patterns get nothing. Don't pretend otherwise in the metrics.
- **Structural transforms.** Reordering, dedup, persona swap, summarization: LCP collapse by construction. New lineage, declared rebuild.
- **Adapter-per-request or absolute-position architectures:** block reuse invalid; budget full prefills.
- **Short contexts:** checkpoint overhead exceeds savings. Enable below a length floor? No — above one.
- **Anchor density tradeoff:** too sparse → cliff-effect reprefills inside a 50k-token tool turn (mitigate with intra-turn anchors at tool-result boundaries); too dense → pinned-block memory pressure and eviction thrash. Tune against measured reuse ratio, alert when it drops below threshold.
- **Multi-tenancy on shared iron:** cross-session block sharing trades hit rate against isolation; namespace radix roots per project unless you've explicitly accepted the timing-channel exposure.

## G. Minimum checkpoint record (if a field is missing, the scheme fails)

```
checkpoint := {
  token_log:        [token ids] + byte-span map,
  anchors:          [{pos, block_refs(pinned, refcounted)}],
  lineage:          {parent_id, epoch, writer},
  fingerprints:     {weights, engine_build, kv_dtype, adapter, template_hash},
  journal_cursor:   side-effect log position,
  open_calls:       issued-but-unresolved tool calls,
  rng_state:        optional, for bit-exact replay,
  checksum:         over all of the above
}
```

Resume algorithm, stated exactly: canonicalize edit → tokenize → token-id LCP against current head's log → deepest anchor with `pos ≤ lcp` and intact fingerprints and live pins → truncate head there → prefill `tokens[lcp:]` at continuing positions → verify final position id → commit new head + journal advance. Any assertion fails → full rebuild from genesis, logged loudly.

The design is sound exactly as far as its discipline: byte-exact identity, quiescent anchors, pinned lifetimes, journaled effects, honest telemetry. Every shortcut in that list converts a visible performance bug into an invisible correctness bug, and on your own iron, there's no vendor to blame.
reasoning:
Let me parse this problem carefully. The user is asking about a hard systems problem: "semantic-anchor checkpoints so an agent's context edit re-prefills only the new suffix, in the operator's own-iron basecamp."

Let me decode the jargon:
- "semantic-anchor checkpoints" — checkpoints in an agent's context/conversation state that are anchored to semantic boundaries (e.g., tool call completions, message boundaries, state transitions) rather than arbitrary token positions.
- "context edit re-prefills only the new suffix" — when the context (prompt/conversation history) is edited, instead of re-sending/re-processing the entire context to the model, you only send the new suffix (the delta). This implies KV-cache reuse / prefix caching semantics. The checkpoint system must ensure that edits preserve the prefix byte-for-byte so the cached KV states remain valid, and only the new suffix gets prefilled.
- "operator's own-iron basecamp" — "own-iron" likely means self-hosted infrastructure ("own iron" = your own hardware), "basecamp" = the operator's home base / local control plane. So this runs on the operator's own hardware, not a third-party API. This matters because it means they control the inference server, can do exact-prefix cache management, but also means no vendor-managed cache invalidation guarantees — they own the failure modes.

So the question: give the edge cases — failure modes, boundaries, and what must never happen.

This is essentially about building a correct incremental-context agent runtime with:
1. Semantic anchors: points in the context stream where a checkpoint can be taken safely (e.g., after a complete assistant turn, after tool results are appended, at stable serialization boundaries).
2. Checkpoints: snapshots of (context bytes, KV-cache block handles/token ids, derived state like scratchpads, file caches).
3. Edit + re-prefill of only the new suffix: when the agent's context changes (e.g., user edits a message, a tool result is revised, memory injection), the system computes the longest common prefix between old and new context, finds the nearest valid semantic anchor at or before that divergence point, truncates the KV cache to that anchor, and prefills only from there.

The hard parts:
- KV cache validity requires exact token-sequence identity of the prefix. Any change upstream invalidates everything downstream.
- Semantic anchors must be chosen such that the anchor point is a place where the serialized context is deterministic and reproducible — i.e., re-serializing the same logical state yields identical bytes.
- Edits can occur anywhere; if an edit occurs before an anchor, all anchors after it are invalidated.
- The "own-iron" part: no external API's implicit caching; you manage paged attention blocks yourself (e.g., vLLM-style prefix caching, SGLang RadixAttention). Cache eviction, block sharing across sessions, fork/branch semantics.

Failure modes to enumerate:

1. **Non-deterministic serialization breaking prefix identity**: If the context serializer includes timestamps, request IDs, random seeds, ordering of dict keys, floating-point formatting, or locale-dependent rendering, then two logically identical states serialize differently → common-prefix computation says divergence earlier than semantically necessary → wasted prefill, or worse, false-positive match if you compare logical hashes instead of bytes.

2. **Hash-vs-bytes mismatch**: Computing the LCP by hashing chunks (e.g., per-message hashes) rather than comparing actual token IDs. A hash collision or a hash computed over normalized text while the tokenizer sees raw bytes → you resume prefill from a token position whose KV states don't correspond to the actual tokens. Silent corruption: the model attends to wrong cached states. Must never happen: resuming from a cache keyed by anything other than the exact token id sequence.

3. **Tokenizer boundary effects**: The suffix boundary may split a multi-token construct. If you truncate at a character/grapheme boundary and re-tokenize, BPE merges across the boundary can produce different token sequences than the original. E.g., editing text such that the last token before the edit point would have merged differently. The anchor must be at a token boundary verified against the original tokenization, and ideally at a semantic boundary where tokenization is guaranteed stable (e.g., start of a message with its role header/delimiter).

4. **Anchor placement inside mutable regions**: An anchor taken mid-tool-call (e.g., after the assistant emitted a partial tool invocation JSON) is not semantically stable — the tool result will be appended, but if the tool call itself gets retried/repaired, the anchor is stale. Anchors must only be placed at quiescent points: completed turns, committed tool results, finalized plan steps.

5. **Edit-before-anchor cascade**: User edits message 3 of 40. All checkpoints after message 3 are invalid. Naive systems keep them and try to salvage via "partial reuse" — impossible for exact-match KV caching. The correct behavior: find deepest surviving anchor ≤ divergence, drop the rest, prefill from there. Failure mode: attempting to splice edited content into cached KV (KV surgery) without a mechanism that accounts for attention over the whole sequence — attention is O(N²) in dependencies; you cannot patch one block's K/V without recomputing attention scores that involve later positions... actually in causal attention, position i's K/V depends only on tokens ≤ i, so if the edit is at position e, all positions ≥ e have K/V values that depend on the edited token through their attention. Wait — no. In causal self-attention, the hidden state at position j is a function of tokens x_0..x_j. So K/V at position j depends on all tokens up to j. Therefore any edit at position e invalidates K/V for all j ≥ e. That's exactly why only-prefix-reuse works and why "suffix reuse" or "middle splice" is unsound. Good — that's a crisp invariant to state: **causal dependency makes every post-edit position's cache entry tainted; there is no sound partial-splice**.

6. **Position-ID / RoPE offset errors**: When resuming prefill from an anchor, positions must continue from the anchor's absolute position. Off-by-one or restarting positions at 0 for the suffix → model sees wrong rotary phases → garbage. Also relevant: sliding-window/attention-sink models where early tokens must remain resident; truncating to an anchor that drops the sink tokens breaks generation entirely.

7. **Cache eviction racing with checkpoint reference**: Own-iron means you run the engine; paged-attention pools evict least-recently-used blocks. If a checkpoint holds references (by block hash) but doesn't pin them, eviction between checkpoint creation and suffix prefill → prefill resumes from missing blocks → either crash or silent fallback to full recompute (correct but slow) — must never silently fall back *without* logging, because that masks perf regressions; worse, some engines return truncated context. Pinning/refcount discipline required.

8. **Cross-session block sharing contamination**: Prefix caching shares blocks by hash across requests/sessions. If sampling-time state (temperature, stop sequences) or system-prompt variants differ but share a prefix hash key that ignores those, you get cross-contamination. Hash key must include everything that affects the forward pass: model revision, quantization config, chat template version, tool-schema serialization, sampler-invariant? Actually sampler doesn't affect prefill KV, but chat template does. Include template hash in the radix key root.

9. **Model/template upgrade mid-session**: Operator updates the model weights or chat template while agents hold checkpoints. Old KV blocks are from different weights — reusing them is silent nonsense. Checkpoints must carry model fingerprint; mismatch → full invalidate.

10. **Quantization/kv-dtype changes**: Same issue — fp16 vs fp8 KV cache blocks aren't interchangeable even with identical token ids.

11. **Semantic anchor defined over logical state, but edit happens at logical layer**: The agent framework edits structured messages (e.g., replaces a tool result object), then re-serializes. If serialization is canonical, fine. If the edit touches a field that serializes into the middle of the byte stream (it always does), the LCP ends there. Edge case: an edit that produces byte-identical output (no-op edit) must be detected and skipped entirely — zero re-prefill. Conversely an edit that only appends should hit the tail anchor with zero dropped work.

12. **Anchors too sparse → cliff effect**: If anchors only exist at turn boundaries and a session has a 50k-token turn (huge tool output), an edit inside that turn forces re-prefill of up to 50k tokens. Mitigation: sub-turn anchors at tool-result boundaries within a turn. Boundary condition: minimum anchor granularity vs. checkpoint storage cost. Each anchor costs metadata + pinned blocks; too many anchors → memory pressure → eviction thrash.

13. **Anchors too dense / checkpoint storm**: Persisting a checkpoint every N tokens creates I/O storms on own-iron disk; async persistence lag means crash recovery rolls back to an older anchor than the live context — then the recovered context diverges from what the agent "remembers" doing (side effects already fired: emails sent, files written). **Context-state vs world-state desync** is a top-tier failure mode: the checkpoint restores context to T, but side effects up to T+k already happened; naive resume re-executes tools → duplicate sends. Need idempotency keys / journaling of side effects alongside context checkpoints, and anchors aligned with the side-effect journal entries (an anchor is only safe to restore-to if all side effects ≤ that anchor are journaled as committed-and-idempotent).

14. **Suffix-only prefill assumes append-only suffix**: If the "edit" is a deletion or replacement that shortens the context, the "new suffix" isn't purely new — it's a divergent continuation. The term "re-prefill only the new suffix" holds only when LCP = old prefix and new content strictly extends it. For replacements, the suffix starts at the divergence point and everything after is recomputed — which is fine, but the failure mode is systems that assume monotonic growth and mis-handle shrinkage (e.g., compaction/summarization passes that rewrite history). Summarization is a wholesale context rewrite → LCP ≈ 0 → full re-prefill; treat as explicit rebuild, never as an incremental edit.

15. **Compaction boundary vs anchor alignment**: Context-window pressure triggers summarization of the oldest k messages. If done naively, the entire remaining context shifts → all caches dead. Correct design: summarize into a fixed-size "genesis block" region and keep the rest byte-stable; or accept full re-prefill as a scheduled, amortized event (do it at idle, not mid-task). Never compact mid-tool-loop.

16. **In-flight generation when edit lands**: Edit arrives while the model is streaming tokens. Tokens already emitted are conditioned on the pre-edit context; the edit invalidates them. You must truncate generated output to the last anchor-compatible point and discard the rest — including any tool calls parsed from discarded text. Failure mode: partially-executed tool call from discarded suffix. What must never happen: executing a tool call whose provenance is invalidated context.

17. **Duplicate-content false LCP**: Repeated boilerplate (system reminders, repeated tool schemas) creates multiple byte-identical regions. A chunk-hash LCP could match at a *later* duplicate occurrence than the true alignment if you align by content alone — no wait, LCP by definition scans from position 0, so duplicates later don't matter for LCP-from-start. But if you implement "find best matching anchor by hash lookup" (radix tree style), a query path could match a different branch with shared prefix — that's fine, radix trees handle it. Real risk: hash-keyed block tables where the key omits position-dependent features (RoPE is relative in most impls so position-independent blocks are OK for full-attention layers, but sliding-window layers and any absolute-position embeddings make blocks position-sensitive). vLLM's prefix caching assumes position-independent blocks — true for standard causal attention with RoPE applied per-position inside the block... Actually RoPE is applied to q/k at their absolute positions; a block's K vectors embed absolute positions. vLLM handles this because reused prefix occupies the same positions. If your edit keeps the prefix identical, positions still align. But if you ever reuse a block at a different offset (dedup of repeated segments mid-stream), RoPE breaks. Must never: reuse KV blocks at shifted offsets for models with absolute position sensitivity (and sliding window attention makes even same-offset reuse tricky across window boundaries — actually SWA blocks depend on a bounded window; prefix reuse still fine since window contents identical).

18. **Multimodal payloads**: Images/PDFs embedded in context. Their tokenization (vision encoder outputs) must be deterministic; preprocessing (resize, normalization) must be versioned. An image re-fetched from disk with different EXIF rotation handling → different embeddings → prefix mismatch despite identical "text." Anchor hashes must cover binary payload digests, not just text.

19. **Tool-result nondeterminism**: A tool result re-executed (retry) returns different bytes (timestamps, IDs). If the framework writes the fresh result into the same slot, LCP breaks at that message even though "semantically" it's the same step. Design choice: freeze first result bytes; retries append as new messages. Otherwise retry storms nuke the cache.

20. **Concurrency: two editors, one context**: Operator basecamp implies possibly multiple panes/scripts mutating the session. Last-writer-wins on the context file while checkpoints were taken under a different writer → anchor table inconsistent with actual bytes. Need single-writer discipline or MVCC with epoch numbers; checkpoints stamped with epoch; stale-epoch checkpoints unusable.

21. **Crash between context commit and checkpoint commit**: Two-phase problem. Order matters: persist checkpoint (bytes+anchor index+block refs) atomically, then advance live pointer. Crash windows leave orphan checkpoints (harmless) or advanced-live-without-checkpoint (must roll back live pointer on recovery). WAL required.

22. **Memory-boundary: anchor beyond free blocks**: Restoring to an anchor whose blocks were evicted → full re-prefill from genesis. Boundaries: define tiered residency — hot (GPU blocks), warm (CPU pinned), cold (disk-backed recompute log). Cold restore = replay token log through prefill, which is just full re-prefill; fine, but must be accounted in latency budgets.

23. **Token-healing / prompt-format drift**: Some frameworks apply "token healing" or trim/repair the prompt (e.g., ensuring assistant turn starts with proper header). If the healer mutates bytes near the suffix boundary, the assumed LCP is wrong. Healing must run before LCP computation, and healed bytes become canonical.

24. **Stop-sequence / partial-token tail**: The last generation may end mid-way with a dangling partial token held in a pending buffer. If the pending buffer is flushed into context later, the checkpoint taken before flush lacks it; LCP computations that include the pending buffer vs ones that don't diverge. Canonical rule: checkpoints only at flushed, finalized boundaries; pending tail is never part of an anchor.

25. **Sampler-state irrelevance but seed-log relevance**: For reproducibility of the suffix continuation, if you need bit-exact regeneration after rollback, you need the RNG seed/log; otherwise rollback+regenerate gives different tokens than the discarded branch — usually acceptable, but for eval harnesses it's a correctness issue.

26. **What must never happen (the hard invariants)**:
   - Never resume prefill from a cache whose key isn't the exact token-id prefix of the current context (byte/token-exact, not semantic-equivalent).
   - Never execute side effects derived from a suffix that was discarded by an edit/rollback.
   - Never mutate a checkpoint in place; checkpoints immutable, edits create new heads.
   - Never let an anchor sit inside a non-quiescent region (mid-tool-call, mid-stream, unflushed pending tokens).
   - Never mix KV blocks across model revisions, dtype, template versions, or quantization configs.
   - Never report cache-hit when falling back to full recompute (telemetry honesty) — and conversely never claim suffix-only prefill when LCP computation failed and you silently did full.
   - Never allow the anchor index to reference unpinned blocks (eviction race).
   - Never apply position offsets incorrectly on resume; assert anchor position == next expected position id.
   - Never trust wall-clock or environment-embedded strings inside serialized context (they break determinism); inject them as explicitly-versioned, frozen-at-write fields.
   - Never compact/summarize transparently as if it were an append; it's a rebuild with a declared discontinuity.

27. **Boundaries (where the technique stops working)**:
   - Edits near the head (early messages): value of suffix-only prefill → zero; full recompute. The economics: savings ∝ length of preserved prefix; edits uniformly distributed → expected preserved fraction ~ position of edit; for long sessions mostly good, for head-heavy edits worthless.
   - Non-append structural transforms (reordering messages, dedup, summarization, persona swap mid-context): LCP collapses; treat as new session lineage.
   - Models/architectures with absolute position embeddings or per-request adapters (LoRA swaps mid-session): block reuse invalid; LoRA change taints all K/V (K/V projections depend on adapter) → full invalidate on adapter switch.
   - Speculative decoding / draft-model caches: separate cache domain; don't conflate.
   - Very short contexts: checkpoint overhead exceeds savings; threshold on context length before enabling anchoring.
   - Multi-agent fan-out where sibling branches share prefixes: beneficial (shared blocks), but refcounting bugs → premature free while a sibling still needs blocks. Refcount must be per-block, atomic, and released only when no live head references it.

28. **Own-iron specifics**: 
   - You control engine version pinning — good, but silent engine upgrades (container retag) change kernel numerics slightly; block hashes keyed on token ids remain valid (KV values differ but that's fine—wait, if weights unchanged, kernels changed → numerics differ slightly; reusing old blocks mixes numeric regimes mid-sequence. Usually tolerable but strictly it's a mixed-numerics hazard; policy: fingerprint engine build in checkpoint, invalidate on mismatch.)
   - Disk-backed checkpoint store on the operator box: fsync discipline; torn writes → corrupt anchor index → must detect via checksums and fall back to older anchor, never to a corrupt one.
   - No vendor rate limits, but own-iron prefill throughput is finite; a bad LCP bug causing full re-prefills of 200k contexts can stall the loop for minutes — observability: track "reuse ratio" per turn; alert below threshold.

29. **LCP computation edge cases**:
   - Comparing token streams, not strings: normalize both sides through the same tokenizer; compute LCP over token ids; map back to anchor table. String-level LCP can land mid-multibyte-character or mid-BPE-merge.
   - Empty suffix (pure no-op): skip prefill entirely; also skip a decode step? No—if the edit is a no-op, nothing to do; don't force a model call.
   - Suffix begins mid-message: allowed only if that message's bytes up to divergence are identical AND the anchor granularity supports intra-message anchors; else roll back to previous message boundary anchor.
   - Unicode normalization: NFC vs NFD differences between editor write and serializer canonical form → spurious divergence at first non-ASCII char. Canonicalize once at ingest.

30. **Checkpoint content completeness**: A checkpoint is more than KV refs: it must capture (a) exact token id list + byte span mapping, (b) anchor position ids, (c) sampled-but-not-yet-committed tail exclusion marker, (d) side-effect journal cursor, (e) open tool-call registry (calls issued, awaiting results), (f) scratchpad/file-watch state if the agent treats local FS as memory, (g) RNG state if reproducibility needed. Missing (e) causes double-execution on restore; missing (d) causes skipped or duplicated effects; missing (a) makes LCP impossible later.

31. **Open tool-call at rollback**: If context rolled back to before a tool call was issued, but the tool already ran (async), the result arrives for a call that no longer exists in context. Policy: quarantine the result, attach to journal, surface to operator; never auto-inject into restored context (would create a phantom message whose provenance predates the head — actually injecting it as a new message is fine semantically but changes LCP; the danger is injecting it into the historical slot).

32. **Time-based fields in system prompt**: "Current time: ..." injected per-call → every call has different prefix → cache useless. Freeze per-session genesis timestamp or move time to a tool. Classic own-goal.

33. **A/B or canary prompts**: Rotating instruction phrasings per turn kills prefix continuity. If experimentation needed, vary only the suffix region.

34. **Boundary of "semantic" anchor definition**: The anchor must be (i) quiescent, (ii) canonically serializable, (iii) at a token boundary, (iv) journaled w.r.t. side effects, (v) pinned in cache. An anchor satisfying only some of these is a trap: e.g., quiescent but not pinned → restore fails; pinned but not quiescent → restoring forks a half-open tool call.

35. **Restore semantics — fork vs rewind**: Rewind (move head back, discard newer) vs fork (keep old head alive, new branch). Own-iron basecamp often wants fork (operator experiments). Fork increases block refcounts; GC must be generational: blocks die when no head in any lineage references them. Leak = GPU OOM hours later; over-free = corruption. This is the classic lifetime bug.

36. **Telemetry/eval integrity**: Metrics computed over "tokens processed" must count reused vs prefilled separately; conflating inflates efficiency claims. And eval harnesses that replay logs must reproduce LCP decisions deterministically — record the LCP decision inputs.

37. **Security-ish edge**: Shared prefix cache across operators' sessions on the same iron — if multi-tenant (even single-operator multi-project), block sharing leaks nothing directly (KV not invertible easily) but timing/cache-side-channels exist; strictest policy: namespace radix roots per session/project. Cost: lower hit rates. Decide explicitly.
